title: Well-Child Care: Growth, Development, Prevention, and Family Priorities at Every Visit
bottomLine: Well-child care is longitudinal prevention, not a checklist of measurements. Review growth and development, feeding/nutrition, sleep, oral health, immunization, injury prevention, family/social context and caregiver concerns while using age-appropriate surveillance and targeted screening rather than indiscriminate testing.
recognize: Growth trajectory matters more than one percentile; developmental progress is interpreted across domains and over time.
differentiate: Normal variants differ from faltering growth, developmental regression and family/environmental barriers that require action.
assessment: Use age-appropriate history/exam, growth plotting, developmental surveillance, family psychosocial assessment and preventive topics guided by the Rourke Baby Record/Greig-type Canadian resources.
workup: Screen hearing, vision, anemia/lead or other conditions only according to age/risk/program recommendations; abnormal growth/development triggers cause-directed evaluation.
management: Provide anticipatory guidance matched to developmental stage and family priorities; close immunization/prevention gaps and refer developmental/social needs early.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine OTC cough/cold medication recommendations in young children and review weight-based dosing carefully when medications are needed.
counselling: Use family-centred, culturally safe guidance and ask what matters most to the caregiver/child rather than delivering a one-way checklist.
followUp: Track unresolved developmental, growth, screening and referral issues longitudinally.
examTrap: Calling a single low percentile growth failure without looking at trajectory—or reassuring developmental regression as normal variation.
oneLinePearl: Well-child care is the trajectory of the child plus the context of the family.
sourceBasis: Rourke Baby Record Canadian preventive-care framework

title: Pediatric Immunization: Use Current NACI Guidance and Continue Interrupted Series
bottomLine: Canadian pediatric immunization is current-guidance work: use the Canadian Immunization Guide/NACI plus the provincial or territorial program, continue rather than restart interrupted series, and adjust for age, immune status, pregnancy, travel/exposure and prior products.
recognize: Schedules differ across provinces and evolve as products/recommendations change; 2026 guidance includes updated RSV, meningococcal and other product changes.
differentiate: National recommendation, product authorization and provincial public funding are not identical concepts.
assessment: Review reliable records, age, immune status, chronic disease, pregnancy where applicable, travel/exposure, prior severe reactions and barriers to access.
workup: Serology is reserved for selected situations; missing records usually lead to catch-up/revaccination according to guidance rather than broad immunity panels.
management: Use current minimum intervals/catch-up schedules and coadminister compatible vaccines when appropriate; do not restart a series because it was delayed.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines may be contraindicated in significant immunosuppression/pregnancy; timing with immune globulin/blood products and some therapies matters.
redFlags: Possible vaccine-preventable disease requiring public-health action
counselling: Address specific concerns respectfully and explain expected reactions versus true contraindications.
followUp: Document and schedule outstanding doses in the applicable provincial/territorial system.
examTrap: Restarting a delayed multidose vaccine series or relying on an old memorized product schedule.
oneLinePearl: Canadian vaccine schedules change; catch up from the doses already given rather than starting over.

title: Newborn Care: Transition, Feeding, Jaundice, Screening, and Early Danger
bottomLine: Newborn care combines physiologic transition with prevention and early detection: assess feeding/hydration/weight, jaundice, cardiorespiratory stability, hip/eye/neurologic exam and completion of provincial metabolic, hearing and critical-congenital-heart screening while escalating temperature instability, respiratory distress, poor feeding or lethargy promptly.
recognize: Normal early weight loss and transitional findings have limits; trajectory and clinical status determine concern.
differentiate: Physiologic jaundice differs from early/rapid/conjugated or illness-associated jaundice; normal sleepiness differs from poor arousability/lethargy.
assessment: Review gestation/birth course, maternal infections/medications, feeding output, weight trend, temperature, color, breathing, tone and family supports.
workup: Ensure provincially required newborn metabolic/hearing/CCHD screening and use bilirubin testing by age in hours/gestational risk when jaundice is present.
management: Support feeding and safe transition; treat hypoglycemia/jaundice/infection or cardiorespiratory problems through newborn-specific pathways and arrange timely follow-up after discharge.
medicationSafety: All newborn medication dosing is weight/gestation-specific; avoid applying older-child dosing or adult formulations.
counselling: Teach safe sleep, feeding/output expectations, jaundice/fever warning signs and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Ensure weight/feeding/jaundice and pending screen results are reviewed promptly after discharge.
examTrap: Calling a sleepy, poorly feeding newborn normal because newborns sleep a lot.
oneLinePearl: In newborns, subtle change in feeding, temperature or arousal can be the first sign of serious disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society newborn care resources

title: Infant Feeding: Growth, Iron, Vitamin D, and Responsive Feeding
bottomLine: Infant feeding assessment is about adequacy and safety, not ideology. Support breastfeeding/chestfeeding and/or formula according to family goals, assess milk transfer and growth, ensure vitamin D/iron guidance appropriate to feeding pattern and age, introduce complementary foods safely and address food insecurity or feeding dysfunction early.
recognize: Output, swallowing/milk transfer, satiety and weight trajectory are more useful than feeding duration alone.
differentiate: Normal cluster feeding differs from inadequate intake/dehydration; reflux/spitting differs from bilious vomiting or feeding-related respiratory symptoms.
assessment: Assess feeding method/frequency, latch or bottle technique, output, weight, prematurity, caregiver goals, supplements, access and signs of aspiration/allergy.
workup: No routine lab panel is needed for a thriving infant; faltering growth or feeding dysfunction triggers targeted evaluation.
management: Provide lactation/formula support, current vitamin D/iron advice and developmentally appropriate complementary foods with allergen introduction according to Canadian guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not dilute formula or use unregulated homemade formula; review medication exposure in lactation with current evidence rather than reflex cessation of breastfeeding.
counselling: Use nonjudgmental language and support safe feeding that works for the family.
followUp: Recheck growth and feeding response after intervention.
examTrap: Judging feeding adequacy from minutes at the breast alone or recommending unsafe formula dilution to save cost.
oneLinePearl: Infant feeding success is adequate growth, hydration and safe responsive feeding—not one feeding method.

title: Growth and Development: Follow the Trajectory, Investigate Regression
bottomLine: Growth and development are longitudinal trajectories. Plot accurate serial measurements, interpret them in family/puberty/medical context, and use developmental milestones as surveillance rather than rigid pass-fail dates; crossing trajectories, loss of skills or disproportionate growth requires evaluation.
recognize: Growth velocity and pattern matter more than one percentile; children can normally track at high or low percentiles.
differentiate: Familial short stature/constitutional delay differs from chronic disease, endocrine disease or undernutrition; developmental variation differs from regression.
assessment: Review prenatal/birth history, nutrition, chronic symptoms, medications, family growth/puberty, developmental domains, school function and psychosocial environment.
workup: Use targeted labs/imaging/genetic/endocrine referral based on growth pattern or developmental findings; broad screening panels are low value without clues.
management: Treat identified medical/nutritional/social causes and refer early intervention/developmental services when delay is persistent or functionally significant.
medicationSafety: Review stimulant, glucocorticoid or other medication effects on growth when clinically relevant.
redFlags: Pubertal progression outside expected pattern with symptoms
counselling: Explain ranges of normal development while taking caregiver concerns seriously.
followUp: Trend objective measures and developmental function rather than relying on one screening result.
examTrap: Calling a child abnormal for being at the 5th percentile despite stable familial growth—or dismissing lost language skills as normal variation.
oneLinePearl: Percentiles are positions; trajectories tell the story.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society developmental and preventive-care resources

title: Developmental Surveillance: Listen to Concerns, Screen Selectively, Refer Early
bottomLine: Developmental surveillance happens at every preventive visit through caregiver concerns, history, observation and milestone trajectory; standardized screening supports but does not replace clinical judgment. Regression, persistent domain delay or concerning autism/neurologic signs should trigger early referral rather than waiting for a definitive label.
recognize: Language, motor, social, cognitive and adaptive skills develop at different rates but should progress over time.
differentiate: Hearing/vision impairment, neurologic disease, autism, global delay, environmental deprivation and language exposure differences can produce different patterns.
assessment: Ask caregiver concerns, observe interaction/play/motor function, review hearing/vision, language exposure, medical history and family/social context.
workup: Use validated age-appropriate screening tools when indicated and targeted hearing/vision/genetic/neurologic evaluation for persistent or global delays.
management: Refer early intervention, speech/OT/PT/developmental pediatrics as indicated without waiting for all etiologic testing to finish.
medicationSafety: Avoid unproven supplements/medications marketed to 'accelerate development' without evidence.
redFlags: No response to sound/major hearing concern
counselling: Explain that early supports can begin before a final diagnosis and are not harmful if the child later catches up.
followUp: Track referral completion and functional progress across domains.
examTrap: Waiting until school age to refer a toddler with persistent language delay because children develop at different rates.
oneLinePearl: Surveillance finds the trajectory; early intervention should not wait for diagnostic perfection.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society developmental surveillance resources

title: Autism Screening: Developmental Pattern, Not One Questionnaire Score
bottomLine: Autism is a neurodevelopmental pattern involving social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours with functional impact. Screening identifies children who need assessment; it does not diagnose autism. Developmental regression, caregiver concern or clear clinical signs warrant referral even if a screen is negative.
recognize: Differences in reciprocal interaction, gestures/language, play, sensory response, repetitive behaviour or insistence on sameness can occur.
differentiate: Hearing loss, language disorder, intellectual disability, ADHD and anxiety can overlap or coexist.
assessment: Review developmental history, regression, language/social communication, play, repetitive/sensory patterns, adaptive function, hearing and family priorities.
workup: Use validated screening tools at recommended ages/when concern arises and arrange formal multidisciplinary/developmental assessment; hearing evaluation is often important.
management: Refer early to supportive developmental/communication/occupational interventions based on functional needs rather than waiting for diagnostic confirmation where services allow.
medicationSafety: Medication does not treat core autism traits; use medications only for defined co-occurring target symptoms with monitoring.
redFlags: Loss of feeding or communication skills
counselling: Use neurodiversity-affirming, non-blaming language and focus support on communication, autonomy and function.
followUp: Track supports, school needs, co-occurring ADHD/anxiety/sleep/feeding issues and caregiver priorities.
examTrap: Treating a negative screening questionnaire as proof autism is absent despite clear developmental concern.
oneLinePearl: Autism screening opens the assessment door; it does not close it.

title: Pediatric ADHD: Developmental History, Multiple Settings, Functional Goals
bottomLine: ADHD is persistent developmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment across settings, with childhood onset. Rating scales support assessment but do not replace developmental, school, sleep, learning, mood, trauma and family evaluation; treatment combines environmental/behavioural supports with medication when indicated.
recognize: Impairment must be more than normal high activity or situational school difficulty.
differentiate: Sleep deprivation, anxiety/depression, trauma, learning disorder, autism, seizures and substance use can mimic or coexist.
assessment: Obtain caregiver/teacher or other setting information, developmental history, school function, sleep, mood/anxiety, trauma, learning, substance risk, cardiovascular history and growth.
workup: No routine brain imaging/lab panel diagnoses ADHD; testing is targeted to mimics/comorbidity.
management: Use classroom/home supports, parent/behaviour strategies and evidence-based stimulant or nonstimulant medication according to age/severity/preferences.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP/HR, appetite, growth, sleep, mood and misuse/diversion; review cardiac red flags before stimulants rather than ordering routine ECG in every child.
counselling: Set functional goals with child/family/school and address safe medication storage.
followUp: Track function/adverse effects rather than rating scores alone.
examTrap: Diagnosing ADHD from one parent questionnaire during untreated sleep deprivation or learning difficulty.
oneLinePearl: ADHD is impairment across settings with developmental history—not a single score.

title: Childhood Asthma: Confirm Variable Disease and Prevent Exacerbations
bottomLine: Pediatric asthma is recurrent variable airflow symptoms with objective confirmation when age permits and a compatible response/pattern in younger children. Control and future exacerbation risk drive ICS-containing management; frequent oral-steroid or ED use means the plan is failing and requires reassessment.
recognize: Wheeze/cough/dyspnea vary with viral illness, exercise, allergens or season; not all preschool wheeze becomes asthma.
differentiate: Foreign body, bronchiolitis, CF, airway anomaly, aspiration and vocal-cord dysfunction can mimic asthma.
assessment: Assess symptoms/night waking/activity, exacerbations, reliever use, triggers, smoke/vape exposure, rhinitis/eczema, adherence and device/spacer technique.
workup: Use spirometry in children able to perform it and age-appropriate diagnostic criteria in preschool children; chest imaging is not routine for typical asthma.
management: Use current Canadian pediatric asthma stepwise ICS-containing therapy, written action plan and inhaler/spacer education; severe exacerbation follows acute asthma pathway.
medicationSafety: LABA is not used without ICS; monitor growth/side effects while recognizing uncontrolled asthma and repeated systemic steroids also harm growth/health.
counselling: Teach child/caregiver action plan, device technique, trigger reduction and when urgent care is needed.
followUp: Reassess control, technique, adherence and exacerbations after therapy changes.
examTrap: Calling every preschool viral wheeze asthma or repeatedly giving oral steroids without a controller/action-plan reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric asthma care prevents the next exacerbation, not just today's wheeze.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute asthma guidance
